question_text: State and prove Bayes' theorem on probability.

mark_split.label: Write P(Eₖ|A) from the conditional probability definition

recall_prompt: Say Bayes' theorem — what the events must be, the formula — then say the two ideas of the proof: the conditional probability definition, and total probability for P(A).
insider_note: The statement must say mutually exclusive AND exhaustive; the proof must show where P(A) comes from. Writing only the formula earns the statement mark and nothing else.

steps.label: State the theorem
steps.margin_note: First mark. Three conditions belong in the statement: E₁, …, Eₙ mutually exclusive, exhaustive, and A an event with P(A) ≠ 0. Then the formula.

lines.text: Statement: If E₁, E₂, …, Eₙ are mutually
exclusive and exhaustive events of a sample
space S, and A is any event with P(A) ≠ 0, then

recall.must_convey: That for mutually exclusive and exhaustive events E₁ to Eₙ and an event A with P(A) ≠ 0, P(Eₖ|A) = P(Eₖ)·P(A|Eₖ) divided by the sum over i of P(Eᵢ)·P(A|Eᵢ).
accept: if E one to E n are mutually exclusive and exhaustive and A is any event then P of E k given A is P E k times P A given E k over the sum of P E i times P A given E i
the probability of E k given A equals P E k P A given E k divided by the total probability of A
bayes theorem gives the posterior of E k as its prior times likelihood over the sum of all prior times likelihood
E one nunchi E n mutually exclusive exhaustive ayithe P of E k given A ante numerator P E k into P A given E k, denominator sum of all
P of E k given A is P E k P A given E k over sigma P E i P A given E i

steps.why: The theorem turns P(A|Eₖ), which the experiment gives, into P(Eₖ|A), which the question asks. The conditions on the Eᵢ are what make the denominator equal to P(A).
common_mistakes: Leaving out "mutually exclusive and exhaustive" — without it P(A) is not the sum.
Writing the denominator as P(A) with no sum shown.
Leaving out P(A) ≠ 0, which the division needs.

steps.label: Use conditional probability
steps.margin_note: Two marks. P(Eₖ|A) = P(Eₖ ∩ A)/P(A) is the definition; the numerator is rewritten by the multiplication theorem as P(Eₖ)·P(A|Eₖ). This is equation (1) and it is what the rest of the proof completes.

lines.text: Proof: By the definition of conditional probability,

recall.must_convey: That P(Eₖ|A) = P(Eₖ ∩ A)/P(A) by definition, and P(Eₖ ∩ A) = P(Eₖ)·P(A|Eₖ) by the multiplication theorem, giving equation (1).
accept: by definition P of E k given A is P of E k intersection A over P A and the numerator is P E k times P A given E k
start from the conditional probability definition and use the multiplication theorem on the intersection
P E k given A equals P E k P A given E k divided by P A which is equation one
conditional probability definition tho start chesi, intersection ni multiplication theorem tho P E k into P A given E k ga rayali
write the conditional probability as intersection over P A then expand the intersection

steps.why: The definition gives a fraction with P(A) below. Everything left to prove is that this P(A) equals the sum in the statement.
common_mistakes: Writing P(Eₖ|A) = P(A|Eₖ) as if the two were equal.
Not naming the multiplication theorem when rewriting P(Eₖ ∩ A).

steps.label: Find P(A) by total probability
steps.margin_note: Three marks — the main step. Because the Eᵢ are exhaustive their union is S, and because they are mutually exclusive the pieces A ∩ Eᵢ are disjoint. So P(A) is the sum of P(A ∩ Eᵢ), and each piece is P(Eᵢ)·P(A|Eᵢ).

lines.text: E₁, …, Eₙ are mutually exclusive and exhaustive,
and A ∩ E₁, A ∩ E₂, …, A ∩ Eₙ are
mutually disjoint (their Eᵢ parts do not meet).
Now A = A ∩ S = A ∩ (E₁ ∪ E₂ ∪ … ∪ Eₙ)

recall.must_convey: That the union of the Eᵢ is S, that the sets A ∩ Eᵢ are disjoint, and so P(A) = Σ P(A ∩ Eᵢ) = Σ P(Eᵢ)·P(A|Eᵢ).
accept: the union of the E i is the whole sample space so A is the union of A intersection E i which are disjoint and P A is the sum of P E i times P A given E i
write A as A intersection S and split it over the exhaustive events then add the disjoint pieces
total probability P of A equals sigma P E i P A given E i
E i lu exhaustive kabatti union S, A ni A intersection E i la ga split chesi, disjoint kabatti add cheyyali
P A is the sum over i of P A intersection E i since the pieces are mutually exclusive

steps.why: Exhaustive makes the union equal S, so A loses nothing when cut along the Eᵢ; mutually exclusive makes the cut pieces disjoint, so their probabilities add. Both conditions in the statement are used here and nowhere else.
common_mistakes: Writing P(A) = Σ P(A ∩ Eᵢ) without saying why the pieces are disjoint.
Skipping A = A ∩ S — the line that brings the Eᵢ in.
Writing P(A ∩ Eᵢ) = P(A)·P(Eᵢ), which needs independence and is not given.

steps.label: Substitute and conclude
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Put (2) into the denominator of (1). The final line must match the statement exactly.

lines.text: (the sum over i = 1 to n). Hence proved.

recall.must_convey: That substituting the total-probability expression for P(A) into equation (1) gives the stated formula.
accept: substitute the total probability for P A in equation one and bayes theorem follows

the denominator becomes sigma P E i P A given E i which is the theorem

steps.why: Equation (1) already had the right numerator; the theorem is proved the moment its denominator is shown to be the sum.
common_mistakes: Ending at equation (2) without writing the final formula.
Writing the final denominator as P(A) instead of the sum.
